not been considered and adopted by the agency at the time of its decision would

delegated to the agency. The Supreme Court’s further suggestion in Chenery I 
that the situation would be far different had the agency formulated a general 
prophylactic rule that it was then applying in this particular reorganization 
gave rise to the subsequent claim that the agency could not act except by 
rulemaking. That position was, of course, rejected in Chenery II, which is also 
reproduced in Chapter 5.
Although the Overton Pork case involved an agency decision for which 
there had been no contemporaneous written explanation, an equally common 
problem facing a reviewing court is a change of rationale for the agency’s 
decision between the tune that it was issued and judicial review. The agency’s 
shift in rationale is, of course, often motivated by cogent objections to its initial 
explanation and offered up in the form of legal argument in court, rather than 
by htigation affidavits, as in Overton Park.

Bad Faith and Department of Commerce v. New York. The Supromp 
Court in Overton Park insisted that judicial review take place based on the 
record that was before the administrator at the time the decision was made 
As the case came before the district court in Overton Park, and subsequently 
to the Supreme Court, the record was incomplete. The remand to the district 
court was for the purpose of producing a more complete record. But, while the 
Court was insistent that review be based on the whole record in order to fully 
understand the administrator’s contemporaneous rationale for the decision, 
the Court warned against further probing the mind of the a dmini stra tor by 
seeking evidence outside of that administrative record. Probing of that sort 
would be appropriate only in circumstances in which the court beheved that 
there had been a strong showing of bad faith on the part of the a dministrator. 
In short, a reviewing court should base its determ in a ti on of the reasonableness 
of an administrator’s contemporaneous rationale on the facts of record before 
the administrator, save in circumstances in which the court beheves that the 
reasons given may be fictitious.
From the time of the Overton Park decision to 2019, the Supreme Court 
did not confront a case with a sufficiently strong showing of “bad faith.” But 
then the Court decided Department of Commerce v. New York, 588 U.S. 752 
(2019). That case involved the decision of the Secretary of Commerce to add a 
citizenship question to the 2020 census questionnaire. Asking about 
citizenship status or place of birth was hardly a novel policy. All but one census
